entries.24e9a14fd3f4c3ac86b3cb9e0d9c83d31bbf9bd4: <div sID="gen6380" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="20" osisID="2Sam.20" sID="2Sam.20"/> <div eID="gen6380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6381" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6382" type="x-p"/> How do the clouds return after the rain! No sooner is one of David's troubles over than another arises, as it were out of the ashes of the former, wherein the threatening is fulfilled, that the sword should never depart from his house. I. Before he reaches Jerusalem a new rebellion is raised by Sheba, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.1-2Sam.20.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. His first work, when he comes to Jerusalem, is to condemn his concubines to perpetual imprisonment, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.3">ver. 3</reference>. III. Amass, whom he entrusts to raise an army against Sheba, is too slow in his motions, which puts him into a fright, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.4-2Sam.20.6">ver. 4-6</reference>. IV. One of his generals barbarously murders the other, when they are taking the field, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.7-2Sam.20.13">ver. 7-13</reference>. V. Sheba is at length shut up in the city of Abel (<reference osisRef="2Sam.20.14-2Sam.20.15">ver. 14, 15</reference>), but the citizens deliver him up to Joab, and so his rebellion is crushed, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.16-2Sam.20.22">ver. 16-22</reference>. The chapter concludes with a short account of David's great officers, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.23-2Sam.20.26">ver. 23-26</reference>.
entries.adaec0402d8ede5b61ef90e241e3cc06285b1812: <div eID="gen6382" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6381" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Sheba's Rebellion. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1023.)</title> <div sID="gen6383" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And there happened to be there a man of Belial, whose name <hi type="italic">was</hi> Sheba, the son of Bichri, a Benjamite: and he blew a trumpet, and said, We have no part in David, neither have we inheritance in the son of Jesse: every man to his tents, O Israel. <hi type="super">2</hi> So every man of Israel went up from after David, <hi type="italic">and</hi> followed Sheba the son of Bichri: but the men of Judah clave unto their king, from Jordan even to Jerusalem. <hi type="super">3</hi> And David came to his house at Jerusalem; and the king took the ten women <hi type="italic">his</hi> concubines, whom he had left to keep the house, and put them in ward, and fed them, but went not in unto them. So they were shut up unto the day of their death, living in widowhood. <div eID="gen6383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6384" type="x-p"/> David, in the midst of his triumphs, has here the affliction to see his kingdom disturbed and his family disgraced. <div eID="gen6384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6385" type="x-p"/> I. His subjects revolting from him at the instigation of <hi type="italic">a man of Belial,</hi> whom they followed when they forsook the <hi type="italic">man after God's own heart.</hi> Observe, 1. That this happened immediately upon the crushing of Absalom's rebellion. We must not think it strange, while we are in this world, if the end of one trouble be the beginning of another: deep sometimes calls unto deep. 2. That the people were now just returning to their allegiance, when, of a sudden, they flew off from it. When a reconciliation is newly made, it ought to be handled with great tenderness and caution, lest the peace break again before it be settled. A broken bone, when it is set, must have time to knot. 3. That the ring-leader of this rebellion was Sheba, a Benjamite by birth (<reference osisRef="2Sam.20.1">v. 1</reference>), who had his habitation in Mount Ephraim, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.21">v. 21</reference>. Shimei and he were both of Saul's tribe, and both retained the ancient grudge of that house. Against the kingdom of the Messiah there is an hereditary enmity in the serpent's seed, and a succession of attempts to overthrow it (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.1-Ps.2.2">Ps. ii. 1, 2</reference>); but he that sits in heaven laughs at them all. 4. That the occasion of it was that foolish quarrel, which we read of in the close of the foregoing chapter, between the elders of Israel and the elders of Judah, about bringing the king back. It was a point of honour that was disputed between them, which had most interest in David. "We are more numerous," say the elders of Israel. "We are nearer akin to him," say the elders of Judah. Now one would think David very safe and happy when his subjects are striving which shall love him best, and be most forward to show him respect; yet even that strife proves the occasion of a rebellion. The men of Israel complained to David of the slight which the men of Judah had put upon them. If he had now countenanced their complaint, commended their zeal, and returned them thanks for it, he might have confirmed them in his interest; but he seemed partial to his own tribe: <hi type="italic">Their words prevailed above the words of the men of Israel;</hi> as some read the last words of the foregoing chapter. David inclined to justify them, and, when the men of Israel perceived this, they flew off with indignation. "If the king will suffer himself to be engrossed by the men of Judah, let him and them make their best of one another, and we will set up one for ourselves. We thought we had ten parts in David, but such an interest will not be allowed us; the men of Judah tell us, in effect, <hi type="italic">we have no part in him,</hi> and therefore we will have none, nor will we attend him any further in his return to Jerusalem, nor own him for our king." This was proclaimed by Sheba (<reference osisRef="2Sam.20.1">v. 1</reference>), who probably was a man of note, and had been active in Absalom's rebellion; the disgusted Israelites took the hint, and <hi type="italic">went up from after David to follow Sheba</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.20.2">v. 2</reference>), that is, the generality of them did so, only the men of Judah adhered to him. Learn hence, (1.) That it is as impolitic for princes to be partial in their attentions to their subjects as it is for parents to be so to their children; both should carry it with an even hand. (2.) Those know not what they do that make light of the affections of their inferiors, by not countenancing and accepting it. Their hatred may be feared whose love is despised. (3.) <hi type="italic">The beginning of strife is as the letting forth of water;</hi> it is <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> wisdom to <hi type="italic">leave it off before it be meddled with,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.17.14">Prov. xvii. 14</reference>. How great a matter doth a little of this fire kindle! (4.) The perverting of words is the subverting of peace; and much mischief is made by forcing invidious constructions upon what is said and written and drawing consequences that were never intended. The men of Judah said, <hi type="italic">The king is near of kin to us.</hi> "By this," say the men of Israel, "you mean that <hi type="italic">we have no part in him;</hi>" whereas they meant no such thing. (5.) People are very apt to run into extremes. <hi type="italic">We have ten parts in David,</hi> said they; and, almost in the next breath, <hi type="italic">We have no part in him.</hi> Today <hi type="italic">Hosanna,</hi> to-morrow <hi type="italic">Crucify.</hi> <div eID="gen6385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6386" type="x-p"/> II. His concubines imprisoned for life, and he himself under a necessity of putting them in confinement, because they had been defiled by Absalom, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.3">v. 3</reference>. David had multiplied wives, contrary to the law and they proved a grief and shame to him. Those whom he had sinfully taken pleasure in he was now, 1. Obliged, in duty, to put away, they being rendered unclean to him by the vile uncleanness his son had committed with them. Those whom he had loved must now be loathed. 2. Obliged, in prudence, to shut up in privacy, not to be seen abroad for shame, lest the sight of them should give occasion to people to speak of what Absalom had done to them, which ought not to be so much as named, <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.1">1 Cor. v. 1</reference>. That that villany might be buried in obscurity. 3. Obliged, in justice to shut up in prison, to punish them for their easy submission to Absalom's lust, despairing perhaps of David's return, and giving him up for gone. Let none expect to do ill and fare well.
entries.61b622060e11badc22e2f969d01983b552135f51: <div eID="gen6386" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Amasa's Death. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1023.)</title> <div sID="gen6387" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> Then said the king to Amasa, Assemble me the men of Judah within three days, and be thou here present. <hi type="super">5</hi> So Amasa went to assemble <hi type="italic">the men of</hi> Judah: but he tarried longer than the set time which he had appointed him. <hi type="super">6</hi> And David said to Abishai, Now shall Sheba the son of Bichri do us more harm than <hi type="italic">did</hi> Absalom: take thou thy lord's servants, and pursue after him, lest he get him fenced cities, and escape us. <hi type="super">7</hi> And there went out after him Joab's men, and the Cherethites, and the Pelethites, and all the mighty men: and they went out of Jerusalem, to pursue after Sheba the son of Bichri. <hi type="super">8</hi> When they <hi type="italic">were</hi> at the great stone which <hi type="italic">is</hi> in Gibeon, Amasa went before them. And Joab's garment that he had put on was girded unto him, and upon it a girdle <hi type="italic">with</hi> a sword fastened upon his loins in the sheath thereof; and as he went forth it fell out. <hi type="super">9</hi> And Joab said to Amasa, <hi type="italic">Art</hi> thou in health, my brother? And Joab took Amasa by the beard with the right hand to kiss him. <hi type="super">10</hi> But Amasa took no heed to the sword that <hi type="italic">was</hi> in Joab's hand: so he smote him therewith in the fifth <hi type="italic">rib,</hi> and shed out his bowels to the ground, and struck him not again; and he died. So Joab and Abishai his brother pursued after Sheba the son of Bichri. <hi type="super">11</hi> And one of Joab's men stood by him, and said, He that favoureth Joab, and he that <hi type="italic">is</hi> for David, <hi type="italic">let him go</hi> after Joab. <hi type="super">12</hi> And Amasa wallowed in blood in the midst of the highway. And when the man saw that all the people stood still, he removed Amasa out of the highway into the field, and cast a cloth upon him, when he saw that every one that came by him stood still. <hi type="super">13</hi> When he was removed out of the highway, all the people went on after Joab, to pursue after Sheba the son of Bichri. <div eID="gen6387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6388" type="x-p"/> We have here Amasa's fall just as he began to rise. He was nephew to David (<reference osisRef="2Sam.17.25">ch. xvii. 25</reference>), had been Absalom's general and commander-in-chief of his rebellious army, but, that being routed, he came over into David's interest, upon a promise that he should be general of his forces instead of Joab. Sheba's rebellion gives David an occasion to fulfil his promise sooner than he could wish, but Joab's envy and emulation rendered its fulfillment of ill consequence both to him and David. <div eID="gen6388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6389" type="x-p"/> I. Amasa has a commission to raise forces for the suppressing of Sheba's rebellion, and is ordered to raise them with all possible expedition, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.4">v. 4</reference>. It seems, the men of Judah, though forward to attend the king's triumphs, were backward enough to fight his battles; else, when they were all in a body attending him to Jerusalem, they might immediately have pursued Sheba, and have crushed that cockatrice in the egg. But most love a loyalty, as well as a religion, that is cheap and easy. Many boast of their being akin to Christ that yet are very loth to venture for him. Amasa is sent to assemble the men of Judah within three days; but he finds them so backward and unready that he cannot do it within the time appointed (<reference osisRef="2Sam.20.5">v. 5</reference>), though the promotion of Amasa, who had been their general under Absalom, was very obliging to them, and a proof of the clemency of David's government. <div eID="gen6389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6390" type="x-p"/> II. Upon Amasa's delay, Abishai, the brother of Joab, is ordered to take the guards and standing forces, and with them to pursue Sheba (<reference osisRef="2Sam.20.6-2Sam.20.7">v. 6, 7</reference>), for nothing could be of more dangerous consequence than to give him time. David gives these orders to Abishai, because he resolves to mortify Joab, and degrade him, not so much, I doubt, for the blood of Abner, which he had shed basely, as for the blood of Absalom, which he had shed justly and honourably. "Now (says bishop Hall) Joab smarteth for a loyal disobedience. How slippery are the stations of earthly honours and subject to continual mutability! Happy are those who are in favour with him in whom there is no shadow of change." Joab, without orders, though in disgrace, goes along with his brother, knowing he might be serviceable to the public, or perhaps now meditating the removal of his rival. <div eID="gen6390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6391" type="x-p"/> III. Joab, near Gibeon, meets with Amasa, and barbarously murders him, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.8-2Sam.20.10">v. 8-10</reference>. It should seem, the great stone in Gibeon was the place appointed for the general rendezvous. There the rivals met; and Amasa, relying upon his commission, went before, as general both of the new-raised forces which he had got together, and of the veteran troops which Abishai had brought in; but Joab there took an opportunity to kill him with his own hand; and, 1. He did it subtilely, and with contrivance, and not upon a sudden provocation. He girded his coat about him, that it might not hang in his way, and girded his belt upon his coat, that his sword might be the readier to his hand; he also put his sword in a sheath too big for it, that, whenever he pleased, it might, upon a little shake, fall out, as if it fell by accident, and so he might take it into his hand, unsuspected, as if he were going to return it into the scabbard, when he designed to sheath it in the bowels of Amasa. The more there is of plot in a sin the worse it is. 2. He did it treacherously, and under pretence of friendship, that Amasa might not be upon his guard. He called him <hi type="italic">brother,</hi> for they were own cousins, enquired of his welfare (<hi type="italic">Art thou in health?</hi>) and <hi type="italic">took him by the beard,</hi> as one he was free with, to kiss him, while with the drawn sword in his other hand he was aiming at his heart. Was this done like a gentleman, like a soldier, like a general? No, but like a villain, like a base coward. Just thus he slew Abner, and went unpunished for it, which encouraged him to do the like again. 3. He did it impudently, not in a corner, but at the head of his troops, and in their sight, as one that was neither ashamed nor afraid to do it, that was so hardened in blood and murders that he could neither blush nor tremble. 4. He did it at one blow, gave the fatal push with a good-will, as we say, so that he needed not strike him again; with such a strong and steady hand he gave this one stroke that it was fatal. 5. He did it in contempt and defiance of David and the commission he had given to Amasa; for that commission was the only ground of his quarrel with him, so that David was struck at through the side of Amasa, and was, in effect, told to his face that Joab would be general, in spite of him. 6. He did it very unseasonably, when they were going against a common enemy and were concerned to be unanimous. This ill-timed quarrel might have scattered their forces, or engaged them one against another, and so have made them all an easy prey to Sheba. So contentedly could Joab sacrifice the interest both of king and kingdom to his personal revenge. <div eID="gen6391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6392" type="x-p"/> IV. Joab immediately resumes his general's place, and takes care to lead the army on in pursuit of Sheba, that, if possible, he might prevent any prejudice to the common cause by what he had done. 1. He leaves one of his men to make proclamation to the forces that were coming up that they were still engaged in David's cause, but under Joab's command, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.11">v. 11</reference>. He knew what an interest he had in the soldiery, and how many favoured him rather than Amasa, who had been a traitor, was now a turn-coat, and had never been successful; on this he boldly relied, and called them all to follow him. What man of Judah would not be for his old king and his old general? But one would wonder with what face a murderer could pursue a traitor; and how, under such a heavy load of guilt, he had courage to enter upon danger. Surely his conscience was seared with a hot iron. 2. Care is taken to remove the dead body out of the way, because at that they made a stand (as <reference osisRef="2Sam.2.23">ch. ii. 23</reference>), and to cover it with a cloth, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.12-2Sam.20.13">v. 12, 13</reference>. Wicked men think themselves safe in their wickedness if they can but conceal it from the eye of the world: if it be hidden, it is with them as if it were never done. But the covering of blood with a cloth cannot stop its cry in God's ear for vengeance, or make it the less loud. However, since this was no time to arraign Joab for what he had done, and the common safety called for expedition, it was prudent to remove that which retarded the march of the army; and then they all went on after Joab, while David, who no doubt had notice soon brought him of this tragedy, could not but reflect upon it with regret that he had not formerly done justice upon Joab for the death of Abner, and that he now had exposed Amasa by preferring him. And perhaps his conscience reminded him of his employing Joab in the murder of Uriah, which had helped to harden him in cruelty.
entries.3b414b5337fc3d10a47c0946b93397f3352a6db8: <div eID="gen6392" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Sheba Pursued. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1023.)</title> <div sID="gen6393" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> And he went through all the tribes of Israel unto Abel, and to Beth-maachah, and all the Berites: and they were gathered together, and went also after him. <hi type="super">15</hi> And they came and besieged him in Abel of Beth-maachah, and they cast up a bank against the city, and it stood in the trench: and all the people that <hi type="italic">were</hi> with Joab battered the wall, to throw it down. <hi type="super">16</hi> Then cried a wise woman out of the city, Hear, hear; say, I pray you, unto Joab, Come near hither, that I may speak with thee. <hi type="super">17</hi> And when he was come near unto her, the woman said, <hi type="italic">Art</hi> thou Joab? And he answered, I <hi type="italic">am he.</hi> Then she said unto him, Hear the words of thine handmaid. And he answered, I do hear. <hi type="super">18</hi> Then she spake, saying, They were wont to speak in old time, saying, They shall surely ask <hi type="italic">counsel</hi> at Abel: and so they ended <hi type="italic">the matter.</hi> <hi type="super">19</hi> I <hi type="italic">am one of them that are</hi> peaceable <hi type="italic">and</hi> faithful in Israel: thou seekest to destroy a city and a mother in Israel: why wilt thou swallow up the inheritance of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ? <hi type="super">20</hi> And Joab answered and said, Far be it, far be it from me, that I should swallow up or destroy. <hi type="super">21</hi> The matter <hi type="italic">is</hi> not so: but a man of mount Ephraim, Sheba the son of Bichri by name, hath lifted up his hand against the king, <hi type="italic">even</hi> against David: deliver him only, and I will depart from the city. And the woman said unto Joab, Behold, his head shall be thrown to thee over the wall. <hi type="super">22</hi> Then the woman went unto all the people in her wisdom. And they cut off the head of Sheba the son of Bichri, and cast <hi type="italic">it</hi> out to Joab. And he blew a trumpet, and they retired from the city, every man to his tent. And Joab returned to Jerusalem unto the king. <div eID="gen6393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6394" type="x-p"/> We have here the conclusion of Sheba's attempt. <div eID="gen6394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6395" type="x-p"/> I. The rebel, when he had rambled over all the tribes of Israel, and found them not so willing, upon second thoughts, to follow him, as they had been upon a sudden provocation to desert David (having only picked up a few like himself, that sided with him), at length entered Abel-Beth-maacah, a strong city in the north, in the lot of Naphtali, where we find it placed, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.29">2 Kings xv. 29</reference>. Here he took shelter, whether by force or with consent does not appear; but his adherents were most Berites, of Beeroth in Benjamin, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.14">v. 14</reference>. One bad man will find or make more. <div eID="gen6395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6396" type="x-p"/> II. Joab drew up all his force against the city, besieged it, battered the wall, and made it almost ready for a general storm, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.15">v. 15</reference>. Justly is that place attacked with all this fury which dares harbour a traitor; nor will that heart fare better which indulges those rebellious lusts that will not have Christ to reign over them. <div eID="gen6396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6397" type="x-p"/> III. A discreet good woman of the city of Abel brings this matter, by her prudent management, to a good issue, so as to satisfy Joab and yet save the city. Here is, <div eID="gen6397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6398" type="x-p"/> 1. Her treaty with Joab, and her capitulation with him, by which he is engaged to raise the siege, upon condition that Sheba be delivered up. It seems, none of all the men of Abel, none of the elders or magistrates, offered to treat with Joab, no, not when they were reduced to the last extremity. They were stupid and unconcerned for the public safety, or they stood in awe of Sheba, or they despaired of gaining any good terms with Joab, or they had not sense enough to manage the treaty. But this one woman and her wisdom saved the city. Souls know no difference of sexes. Though the man be the head, it does not therefore follow that he has the monopoly of the brains, and therefore he ought not, by any salique law, to have the monopoly of the crown. Many a masculine heart, and more than masculine, has been found in a female breast; nor is the treasure of wisdom the less valuable for being lodged in the weaker vessel. In the treaty between this nameless heroine and Joab, <div eID="gen6398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6399" type="x-p"/> (1.) She gains his audience and attention, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.16-2Sam.20.17">v. 16, 17</reference>. We may suppose it was the first time he had ever treated with a woman in martial affairs. <div eID="gen6399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6400" type="x-p"/> (2.) She reasons with him on behalf of her city, and very ingeniously. [1.] That it was a city famous for wisdom (<reference osisRef="2Sam.20.18">v. 18</reference>), as we translate it. She pleads that this city had been long in such reputation for prudent knowing men that it was the common referee of the country, and all agreed to abide by the award of its elders. Their sentence was an oracle; let them be consulted and the matter is ended, all sides will acquiesce. Now shall such a city as this be laid in ashes and never treated with? [2.] That the inhabitants were generally peaceable and faithful in Israel, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.19">v. 19</reference>. She could speak, not for herself only, but for all those whose cause she pleaded, that they were not of turbulent and seditious spirits, but of known fidelity to their prince and peaceableness with their fellow-subjects; they were neither seditious nor litigious. [3.] That it was a mother in Israel, a guide and nurse to the towns and country about; and that it was a part of <hi type="italic">the inheritance of the Lord,</hi> a city of Israelites, not of heathen; and the destruction of it would lessen and weaken that nation which God had chosen for his heritage. [4.] That they expected him to offer them peace before he made an attack upon the, according to that known law of war, <reference osisRef="Deut.20.10">Deut. xx. 10</reference>. So the margin reads (<reference osisRef="2Sam.20.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">They plainly spoke in the beginning</hi> (of the siege), <hi type="italic">saying, Surely they will ask of Abel,</hi> that is, "The besiegers will demand the traitor, and will ask us to surrender him; and if they do, we will soon come to an agreement, and so end the matter." Thus she tacitly upbraids Joab for not offering them peace, but hopes it is not too late to beg it. <div eID="gen6400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6401" type="x-p"/> (3.) Joab and Abel's advocate soon agree that Sheba's head shall be the ransom of the city. Joab, though in a personal quarrel he had lately swallowed up and destroyed Amasa, yet, when he acts as a general, will by no means bear the imputation of delighting in bloodshed: "<hi type="italic">Far be it from me that I should</hi> delight to <hi type="italic">swallow up or destroy,</hi> or design it but when it is necessary for the public safety, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.20">v. 20</reference>. The matter is not so. Our quarrel is not with your city; we would hazard our lives for its protection. Our quarrel is only with the traitor that is harboured among you; deliver him up, and we have done." A great deal of mischief would be prevented if contending parties would but understand one another. The city obstinately holds out, believing Joab aims at its ruin. Joab furiously attacks it, believing the citizens all confederates with Sheba. Whereas both were mistaken; let both sides be undeceived, and the matter is soon accommodated. The single condition of peace is the surrender of the traitor. It is so in God's dealing with the soul, when it is besieged by conviction and distress: sin is the traitor; the beloved lust is the rebel; part with that, cast away the transgression, and all shall be well. No peace on any other terms. Our wise woman immediately agrees to the proposal: <hi type="italic">Behold, his head shall be thrown to thee presently.</hi> <div eID="gen6401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6402" type="x-p"/> 2. Her treaty with the citizens. She went to them in her wisdom (and perhaps she had as much need of it in dealing with them as in dealing with Joab) and persuaded them to cut off Sheba's head, probably by some public order of their government, and it was thrown over the wall to Joab. He knew the traitor's face, and therefore looked no further, intending not that any of his adherents should suffer. The public safety was secured, and he felt no wish to gratify the public revenge. Joab hereupon raised the siege, and marched back to Jerusalem, with the trophies rather of peace than victory.
entries.98d355bc1f09255932c9edd1bcf7cfc471107d20: <div eID="gen6402" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David's Court. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1023.)</title> <div sID="gen6403" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> Now Joab <hi type="italic">was</hi> over all the host of Israel: and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada <hi type="italic">was</hi> over the Cherethites and over the Pelethites: <hi type="super">24</hi> And Adoram <hi type="italic">was</hi> over the tribute: and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud <hi type="italic">was</hi> recorder: <hi type="super">25</hi> And Sheva <hi type="italic">was</hi> scribe: and Zadok and Abiathar <hi type="italic">were</hi> the priests: <hi type="super">26</hi> And Ira also the Jairite was a chief ruler about David. <div eID="gen6403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6404" type="x-p"/> Here is an account of the state of David's court after his restoration. Joab retained the office of general, being too great to be displaced. Benaiah, as before, was captain of the guards. Here is one new office erected, which we had not (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.16-2Sam.8.18">ch. viii. 16-18</reference>), that of <hi type="italic">treasurer,</hi> or one <hi type="italic">over the tribute,</hi> for it was not till towards the latter end of his time that David began to raise taxes. Adoram was long in this office, but it cost him his life at last, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.18">1 Kings xii. 18</reference>.  <chapter eID="2Sam.20"/> <div eID="gen6404" type="x-p"/>

entries.29c88f1358845ed2f6a8715780624c1da0afab89: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3020"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 20</title> <div sID="gen4177" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.1-2Sam.20.9">2Sa 20:1-9</reference>. Sheba Makes a Party in Israel.<div eID="gen4177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4178" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3020"/><hi type="bold">1. Sheba ... a Benjamite--</hi>Though nothing is known of this man, he must have been a person of considerable power and influence, before he could have raised so sudden and extensive a sedition. He belonged to the tribe of Benjamin, where the adherents of Saul's dynasty were still numerous; and perceiving the strong disgust of the other tribes with the part assumed by Judah in the restoration, his ill-designing heart resolved to turn it to the overthrow of David's authority in Israel.<div eID="gen4178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4179" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">every man to his tents--</hi>This proverbial expression may have had its foundation in the fact, that many of the Israelite peasantry adhered to the custom of the patriarchs who tilled land, and yet lived in tents, as Syrian peasants often do still. This was the usual watchword of national insurrection, and from the actual temper of the people, it was followed by effects beyond what he probably anticipated. <div eID="gen4179" type="x-p"/>
entries.08d5b622f9d0b34458c6b628bce49ac85e75efd9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3021"/><div sID="gen4180" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3021"/><hi type="bold">2. from Jordan even to Jerusalem--</hi>The quarrel had broken out shortly after the crossing of the Jordan, between Judah and the other tribes, who withdrew; so that Judah was left nearly alone to conduct the king to the metropolis. <div eID="gen4180" type="x-p"/>
entries.8faf829f06629e5beef671032769372a7ed25dfa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3022"/><div sID="gen4181" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3022"/><hi type="bold">3. the king took the ten women his concubines--</hi>Jewish writers say that the widowed queens of Hebrew monarchs were not allowed to marry again but were obliged to pass the rest of their lives in strict seclusion. David treated his concubines in the same manner after the outrage committed on them by Absalom. They were not divorced, for they were guiltless; but they were no longer publicly recognized as his wives; nor was their confinement to a sequestered life a very heavy doom, in a region where women have never been accustomed to go much abroad. <div eID="gen4181" type="x-p"/>
entries.9e6efb06520983b1d0298eb0630611189b34f507: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3023"/><div sID="gen4182" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3023"/><hi type="bold">4. Then said the king to Amasa, Assemble me the men of Judah within three days--</hi>Amasa is now installed in the command which David had promised him. The revolt of the ten tribes, probably, hastened the public declaration of this appointment, which he hoped would be popular with them, and Amasa was ordered within three days to levy a force from Judah sufficient to put down the insurrection. The appointment was a blunder, and the king soon perceived his error. The specified time passed, but Amasa could not muster the men. Dreading the loss of time, the king gave the commission to Abishai, and not to Joab--a new affront, which, no doubt, wounded the pride of the stern and haughty old general. But he hastened with his attached soldiers to go as second to his brother, determined to take the first opportunity of wreaking his vengeance on his successful rival. <div eID="gen4182" type="x-p"/>
entries.f4534effb273cce99ebe656a4f21d821ff2fd7c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3024"/><div sID="gen4183" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3024"/><hi type="bold">8. Amasa went before them--</hi>Having collected some forces, he by a rapid march overtook the expedition at Gibeon, and assumed the place of commander; in which capacity, he was saluted, among others, by Joab.<div eID="gen4183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4184" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Joab's garment, that he had put on was girded unto him--</hi>in the fashion of travellers and soldiers.<div eID="gen4184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4185" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a sword ... and as he went forth it fell out--</hi>that is, out of the scabbard. According to Josephus, he let it drop on purpose as he was accosting Amasa, that stooping, as it were accidentally, to pick it up, he might salute the new general with the naked sword in his hand, without exciting any suspicion of his design.<div eID="gen4185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4186" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">He went forth--</hi>in a ceremonious manner to meet Amasa, now commander-in-chief, in order to seem to render to that officer, whom he considered as usurping his post, a conspicuous honor and homage. <div eID="gen4186" type="x-p"/>
entries.beece493309a77282b9e2ee18fa3feb09e13e1b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3025"/><div sID="gen4187" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3025"/><hi type="bold">9. took Amasa by the beard with the right hand to kiss him--</hi>This act, common with two friends on meeting when one of them returns from a journey, indicates respect as well as kindliness, and the performance of it evinced the deep hypocrisy of Joab, who thereby put Amasa off his guard. No wonder, then, that while this act of friendly gratulation after long absence occupied Amasa's attention, he did not perceive the sword that was in Joab's left hand. The action of Joab was indeed a high compliment, but neither suspicious nor unusual and to this compliment, Amasa paying attention and no doubt returning it with suitable politeness, he could little expect the fatal event that Joab's perfidy produced.<div eID="gen4187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4188" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.10-2Sam.20.13">2Sa 20:10-13</reference>. Amasa Is Slain. <div eID="gen4188" type="x-p"/>
entries.befe5c19a7120b69dd351b7996521b4e45a31682: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3026"/><div sID="gen4189" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3026"/><hi type="bold">10. smote him ... in the fifth rib--</hi>the seat of the liver and bowels, where wounds are mortal.<div eID="gen4189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4190" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">struck him not again--</hi>that is, despatched him at the first blow. <div eID="gen4190" type="x-p"/>
entries.ab03e9118b647aae256256715cba4289745c67d0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3027"/><div sID="gen4191" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3027"/><hi type="bold">11-13. He that favoureth Joab, and he that is for David, let him go after Joab--</hi>It is a striking proof of Joab's unrivalled influence over the army, that with this villainous murder perpetrated before their eyes they unanimously followed him as their leader in pursuit of Sheba. A soldier conjoined his name with David's, and such a magic spell was in the word "Joab," that all the people "went on"--Amasa's men as well as the rest. The conjunction of these two names is very significant. It shows that the one could not afford to do without the other--neither Joab to rebel against David, nor David to get rid of Joab, though hating him.<div eID="gen4191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4192" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.14">2Sa 20:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.15">15</reference>. Joab Pursues Sheba unto Abel. <div eID="gen4192" type="x-p"/>
entries.9437250cbdca23c127db23f9f7ac3c26c6367aa4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3028"/><div sID="gen4193" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3028"/><hi type="bold">14. he went through all the tribes of Israel unto Abel--</hi>beating up for recruits. But there the prompt marches of Joab overtook and hemmed him in by a close siege of the place. <div eID="gen4193" type="x-p"/>
entries.61bde2830ed72258febb502e9f473d7143980927: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3029"/><div sID="gen4194" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3029"/><hi type="bold">15. Abel of Beth-maachah--</hi>a verdant place--the addition of "Maachah" betokening that it belonged to the district Maachah, which lay far up the Jordan at the foot of Lebanon.<div eID="gen4194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4195" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.16-2Sam.20.22">2Sa 20:16-22</reference>. A Wise Woman Saves the City by Sheba's Head. <div eID="gen4195" type="x-p"/>
entries.ae4321788d8efebbe65a4d2b34f3bac9b43aeb3c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3030"/><div sID="gen4196" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3030"/><hi type="bold">16. Then cried a wise woman--</hi>The appeal of this woman, who, like Deborah, was probably a judge or governess of the place, was a strong one. <div eID="gen4196" type="x-p"/>
entries.ec410da2111463f33924fb090fc05ec21cc0ba29: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3031"/><div sID="gen4197" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3031"/><hi type="bold">18-20. They were wont to speak in old time--</hi>The translation of the Margin gives a better meaning, which is to this effect: When the people saw thee lay siege to Abel, they said, Surely he will ask if we will have peace, for the law (<reference osisRef="Deut.20.10">De 20:10</reference>) prescribes that he should offer peace to strangers, much more then to Israelitish cities; and if he do this, we shall soon bring things to an amicable agreement, for we are a peaceable people. The answer of Joab brings out the character of that ruthless veteran as a patriot at heart, who, on securing the author of this insurrection, was ready to put a stop to further bloodshed and release the peaceable inhabitants from all molestation.<div eID="gen4197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4198" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.23-2Sam.20.26">2Sa 20:23-26</reference>. David's Great Officers. <div eID="gen4198" type="x-p"/>
entries.b97bb28e9359655df304505f08e35362f4c96571: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3032"/><div sID="gen4199" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3032"/><hi type="bold">23. Now Joab was over all the host of Israel--</hi>David, whatever his private wishes, found that he possessed not the power of removing Joab; so winking at the murder of Amasa, he re-established that officer in his former post of commander-in-chief. The enumeration of David's cabinet is here given to show that the government was re-established in its wonted course. <chapter eID="2Sam.20"/>

entries.735529d2045e336b511aa7d473918253842641fe: <div eID="gen11249" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen11250" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11251" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11251" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11250" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11252" type="x-p"/> Sheba raises an insurrection, and gains a party in Israel, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.1">2Sam 20:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.2">2Sam 20:2</reference>. David shuts up the ten concubines who were defiled by Absalom, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.3">2Sam 20:3</reference>. Amasa is sent to assemble the men of Judah, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.4">2Sam 20:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.5">2Sam 20:5</reference>. And in the mean time Abishai is sent to pursue Sheba, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.6">2Sam 20:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.7">2Sam 20:7</reference>. Joab treacherously murders Amasa, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.8-2Sam.20.12">2Sam 20:8-12</reference>. Joab and the army continue the pursuit of Sheba, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.13">2Sam 20:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.14">2Sam 20:14</reference>. He is besieged in Abel; and, by the counsels of a wise woman, the people of Abel cut off his head, and throw it over the wall to Joab; who blows the trumpet of peace, and he and his men return to Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.15-2Sam.20.22">2Sam 20:15-22</reference>. Account of David's civil and military officers, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.23-2Sam.20.26">2Sam 20:23-26</reference>. <div eID="gen11252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11253" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen11253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11254" type="x-p"/> Sheba, the son of Bichri - As this man was a Benjamite, he probably belonged to the family of Saul; and he seems to have had considerable influence in Israel to raise such an insurrection: but we know nothing farther of him than what is related in this place. <div eID="gen11254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11255" type="x-p"/> We have no part in David - We of Israel, we of the ten tribes, are under no obligation to the house of David. Leave him, and let every man fall into the ranks under his own leader.
entries.164c22051214ac243f38411f2c016074ebc440d1: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen11255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11256" type="x-p"/> The ten women - He could not well divorce them; he could not punish them, as they were not in the transgression; he could no more be familiar with them, because they had been defiled by his son; and to have married them to other men might have been dangerous to the state: therefore he shut them up and fed them - made them quite comfortable, and they continued as widows to their death.
entries.684d054bd0567a6f5e3c8944a65a3fb2b0739f70: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen11256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11257" type="x-p"/> Then said the king to Amasa - Thus he invests him with the command of the army, and sends him to collect the men of Judah, and to come back to receive his orders in relation to Sheba, in three days. It appears that Amasa found more difficulty in collecting his country-men than was at first supposed; and this detaining him beyond the three days, David, fearing that Sheba's rebellion would get head, sent Abishai, who it appears was accompanied by Joab, to pursue after Sheba. <div eID="gen11257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11258" type="x-p"/> Amasa, it seems, got up with them at Gibeon, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.8">2Sam 20:8</reference>, where he was treacherously murdered by the execrable Joab.
entries.48ea5a736bb56777e1652e2a48ceb45203f91ad6: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen11258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11259" type="x-p"/> Joab's garment - It appears that this was not a military garment; and that Joab had no arms but a short sword, which he had concealed in his girdle; and this sword, or knife, was so loose in its sheath that it could be easily drawn out. It is thought farther, that Joab, in passing to Amasa, stumbled, (for so some of the versions, and able critics, understand the words it fell out). and that the sword fell down when he stumbled; that he took it up with his left hand as if he had no bad intention; and then, taking Amasa by the beard with his right hand, pretending to kiss him, he, with his sword in his left hand, ripped up his bowels. This seems to be the meaning of this very obscure verse. It is worthy of remark that in the Eastern country it is the beard, not the man, which is usually kissed.
entries.43bb40c4c3f183b5cacd7c4d1d9597873aca45e8: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen11259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11260" type="x-p"/> In the fifth rib - I believe חמש chomesh, which we render here and elsewhere the fifth rib, means any part of the abdominal region. The Septuagint translate it την ψοαν, the groin; the Targum, the right side of the thigh, i.e., (the phrase of the Targumist being interpreted), the privy parts. That it means some part of the abdominal region, is evident from what follows, And shed out his bowels to the ground. It appears from this that, in plain English, he ripped up his belly.
entries.200e7a40e07c19fc5ca49234a1c0982035b949f6: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen11260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11261" type="x-p"/> He that favoureth Joab - As if he had said, There is now no other commander besides Joab; and Joab is steadily attached to David: let those therefore who are loyal follow Joab.
entries.354e72507efbbfd5dfd5eda8800ab9a579d18d8e: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen11261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11262" type="x-p"/> Amasa wallowed in blood - It is very likely that Amasa did not immediately die; I have known instances of persons living several hours after their bowels had been shed out.
entries.97280ed54b45884dad075e0538952da4fdb23902: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen11262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11263" type="x-p"/> Unto Abel - This is supposed to have been the capital of the district called Abilene in St. Luke's Gospel, <reference osisRef="Luk.3.1">Luk 3:1</reference>. <div eID="gen11263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11264" type="x-p"/> Beth-maachah - Is supposed to have been in the northern part of the Holy Land, on the confines of Syria, and probably in the tribe of Naphtali.
entries.2dcfd06939bac973c5c9b99ce752037d1c48a5ef: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen11264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11265" type="x-p"/> They cast up a bank against the city - The word סללה solelah, which we render bank, means, most probably, a battering engine of some kind, or a tower overlooking the walls, on which archers and slingers could stand and annoy the inhabitants, while others of the besiegers could proceed to sap the walls. That it cannot be a bank that stood in the trench, is evident from the circumstance thus expressed.
entries.1bea0c4d21a91de343b0f3c45daac2a74b8cff81: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen11265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11266" type="x-p"/> A wise woman - She was probably governess.
entries.61c28d6696986838e60d35cac7b6ab2bc6467811: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen11266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11267" type="x-p"/> They shall surely ask counsel at Abel - This is a proverb, but from what it originated we know not; nor can we exactly say what it means: much must be supplied to bring it to speak sense. Abel was probably famed for the wisdom of its inhabitants; and parties who had disputes appealed to their judgment, which appears to have been in such high reputation as to be final by consent of all parties. To this the wise woman refers, and intimates to Joab that he should have proceeded in this way before he began to storm the city, and destroy the peaceable inhabitants.
entries.01c752ebf94fb16510b95f1e619e1a8ba6f8f32b: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen11267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11268" type="x-p"/> I - peaceable and faithful in Israel - I am for peace, not contention of any kind; I am faithful - I adhere to David, and neither seek nor shall sanction any rebellion or anarchy in the land. Why then dost thou proceed in such a violent manner? Perhaps the woman speaks here in the name and on behalf of the city: "I am a peaceable city, and am faithful to the king." <div eID="gen11268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11269" type="x-p"/> A mother in Israel - That is, a chief city of a district; for it is very likely that the woman speaks of the city, not of herself.
entries.573d042f9bf4108a91f4c323fd634e08fd34aafb: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen11269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11270" type="x-p"/> His head shall be thrown to thee - Thus it appears she had great sway in the counsels of the city; and that the punishment of a state rebel was then, what it is now in this kingdom, beheading.
entries.637bd123bb515dd748b990e42ee496028bbaaba1: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen11270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11271" type="x-p"/> Joab was over all the host - He had murdered Amasa, and seized on the supreme command: and such was his power at present, and the service which he had rendered to the state by quelling the rebellion of Sheba, that David was obliged to continue him; and dared not to call him to account for his murders without endangering the safety of the state by a civil war. <div eID="gen11271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11272" type="x-p"/> Benaiah - over the Cherethites - Benaiah was over the archers and slingers. <div eID="gen11272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11273" type="x-p"/> See the notes on <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.18">2Sam 8:18</reference>.
entries.714e51a12b9561a5a500044e8b5404df5584e609: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen11273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11274" type="x-p"/> Adoram was over the tribute - Probably the chief receiver of the taxes; or Chancellor of the Exchequer, as we term it. <div eID="gen11274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11275" type="x-p"/> Jehoshaphat - recorder - The registrar of public events.
entries.49018a36d256c3746f0d9c0db8d21ad8ce7c2f5a: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen11275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11276" type="x-p"/> Shevah was scribe - The king's secretary.
entries.609fbffff27c1681a5459ef4e3305cee341f734e: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen11276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11277" type="x-p"/> Ira - was a chief ruler about David - The Hebrew is כהן לדויד cohen ledavid, a priest to David; and so the Vulgate, Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic. The Chaldee has רב rab, a prince, or chief. He was probably a sort of domestic chaplain to the king. We know that the kings of Judah had their seers, which is nearly the same: Gad was David's seer, <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.11">2Sam 24:11</reference>, and Jeduthun was the seer of King Josiah, <reference osisRef="2Chr.35.16">2Chr 35:16</reference>. <div eID="gen11277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11278" type="x-p"/> The conclusion of this chapter is very similar to the conclusion of <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.16-2Sam.8.18">2Sam 8:16-18</reference> (note), where see the notes.  <chapter eID="2Sam.20"/> <div eID="gen11278" type="x-p"/>

entries.7ada0343987849e8a0cc0695bb4c245ca88410bd: Sheba’s Rebellion. - 2Sa 20:1. There happened to be a worthless man there, named <hi type="italic">Sheba</hi>, a Benjaminite. He blew the trumpet, and said, “We have no part in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse. Every man to his tents, O Israel!” <hi type="italic">“To his tents,”</hi> i.e., to his home, as in <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.9">2Sa 19:9</reference>, etc.
entries.a5f24ce43605faf91b0d9d48ee55943c8588bdab: <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.2">2Sa 20:2</reference> <div eID="gen4532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4533" type="x-p"/> All the men of Israel responded to this call, and went up (to the mountains) away from David and after Sheba; but the men of Judah adhered to their king from the Jordan to Jerusalem. The construction of דּבק with ועד ... מן is a pregnant one: they adhered to and followed him. The expression <hi type="italic">“from Jordan”</hi> does not prove that Sheba’s rebellion broke out at the Jordan itself, and before David’s arrival in Gilgal, but may be accounted for from the fact that the men of Judah had already fetched the king back across the Jordan.
entries.120fe7d58b86b28084b6f7f55ae498c89ec53df5: <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.3">2Sa 20:3</reference> <div eID="gen4533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4534" type="x-p"/> As soon as David returned to his palace at Jerusalem, he brought the ten concubines whom he had left behind, and with whom Absalom had lain, into a place of safety, and took care of them, without going in unto them any more. The masculine suffixes attached to יתּגם, יכלכּלם, and אליהם are used, as they frequently are, as being the more general and indefinite, instead of the feminine, which is the more definite form. Thus were they shut up in lifelong widowhood until the day of their death. אלמנוּת is an adverbial accusative, and חיּוּת signifies “condition in life;” literally, in widowhood of life.
entries.b97ccac87357e6a380c97fc3a406ab995c66a1ce: <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.4">2Sa 20:4</reference> <div eID="gen4534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4535" type="x-p"/> David then ordered Amasa to call the men of Judah to pursue Sheba the rebel, and attack him within three days, and then to present himself to him again. This commission was intended as the commencement of the fulfilment of the promise which David had given to Amasa (<reference osisRef="2Sam.19.14">2Sa 19:14</reference>). It was no doubt his intention to give him the command over the army that marched against Sheba, and after the defeat of the rebel to make him commander-in-chief. But this first step towards the fulfilment of the promise was a very imprudent act, like the promise itself, since Joab, who had been commander of the army for so many years, was grievously offended by it; and moreover, being a well-tried general, he had incomparably more distinction in the tribe of Judah than Amasa, who had taken part in Absalom’s rebellion and even led the rebel army, could possibly have.
entries.533ba428767ecda6d250cd49c507cf237844ce32: <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.5-2Sam.20.6">2Sa 20:5-6</reference> <div eID="gen4535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4536" type="x-p"/> But when Amasa stayed out beyond the time fixed for the execution of the royal commission (the <hi type="italic">Chethib</hi> וייחר is the <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> וייחר, whilst the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> is either the <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> ויּוחר, or the imperfect <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> of יחר = אחר, cf. תּחז, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.9">2Sa 20:9</reference>, and is quite unnecessary), probably because the men of Judah distrusted him, and were not very ready to respond to his summons, David said to Abishai, “Now will Sheba the son of Bichri be more injurious (more dangerous) to us than Absalom. Take thou the servants (soldiers) of thy lord and pursue after him, lest he reach fortified cities, and <hi type="italic">tear out our eye</hi>,” i.e., do us a serious injury. This is the correct explanation given by Böttcher, who refers to <reference osisRef="Deut.32.10">Deu 32:10</reference> and Zec 2:12, where the apple of the eye is the figure used to signify the most valuable possession; for the general explanation, “and withdraw from our eye,” cannot be grammatically sustained.
entries.98dc597582eedc9a3fe58b8d0144aca13f3acd5d: <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.7">2Sa 20:7</reference> <hi type="italic">Thus there went after him</hi> (Abishai) <hi type="italic">Joab’s men</hi> (the corps commanded by Joab), <hi type="italic">and the Crethi and Plethi </hi>(see at <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.18">2Sa 8:18</reference>), out of Jerusalem, to pursue Sheba.
entries.804197ded91a0f35b985edd2427f436e38de7bab: <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.8">2Sa 20:8</reference> “When they were by the great stone at Gibeon, and Amasa came to meet them (there), Joab was girded with his armour-coat as his clothing, and the girdle of the sword was bound over it upon his loins in its sheath, which came out, and it fell (i.e., the sheath came out of the sword-belt in which it was fastened, and the sword fell to the ground), Joab said to Amasa,” etc. The eighth verse contains only circumstantial clauses, the latter of which (from ויואב onwards) are subordinate to the earlier ones, so that ויּאמר (<reference osisRef="2Sam.20.9">2Sa 20:9</reference>) is attached to the first clause, which describes the meeting between the advancing army and Amasa. <div eID="gen4536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4537" type="x-p"/> There is something striking, however, in the fact that Joab appears among them, and indeed, as we see from what follows, as the commander of the forces; for according to <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.6">2Sa 20:6</reference>, David had commissioned Abishai, Joab’s brother, to pursue Sheba, and even in <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.7">2Sa 20:7</reference> Joab’s men only are mentioned. This difficulty can hardly be solved in any other manner than by the simple assumption that David had told Abishai to go out with Joab, and that this circumstance is passed over in the brief account in <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.6">2Sa 20:6</reference>, in which the principal facts alone are given, and consequently the name of Joab does not occur there. Clericus adopts the following explanation. “Mention,” he says, “has hitherto been made simply of the command given to Abishai, but this included an order to Joab to go as well; and there is nothing to preclude the supposition that Joab’s name was mentioned by the king, although this is not distinctly stated in the brief account before us.”<note placement="foot">This difficulty cannot be removed by emendations of the text, inasmuch as all the early translators, with the exception of the Syriac, had our Hebrew text before them. Thenius does indeed propose to alter <hi type="italic">Abishai</hi> into <hi type="italic">Joab</hi> in <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.6">2Sa 20:6</reference>, after the example of Josephus and the Syriac; but, as Böttcher observes, if <hi type="italic">Joab</hi> had originally formed part of the text, it could not have been altered into Abishai either accidentally or intentionally, and the Syriac translators and Josephus have inserted <hi type="italic">Joab</hi> merely from conjecture, because they inferred from what follows that Joab’s name ought to be found here. But whilst this is perfectly true, there is no ground for Böttcher’s own conjecture, that in the original text <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.6">2Sa 20:6</reference> read as follows: “Then David said to Joab, Behold, the three days are gone: shall we wait for Amasa?” and through the copyist’s carelessness a whole line was left out. For this conjecture has no tenable support in the senseless reading of the <hi type="italic">Cod. Vat</hi>., πρὸς Ἀμεσσαΐ́ for Ἀβισαΐ́.</note>
entries.5dc8f9ecf46dd629fa517021d219ba9c8d075198: <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.9-2Sam.20.10">2Sa 20:9-10</reference> <div eID="gen4537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4538" type="x-p"/> Joab asked Amasa how he was, and laid hold of his bear with his right hand to kiss him. And as Amasa took no heed of the sword in Joab’s hand, he smote him with it in the paunch (abdomen), and shed out his bowels upon the ground, “<hi type="italic">and repeated not</hi> (the stroke) <hi type="italic">to him</hi>” (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.8">1Sa 26:8</reference>). Laying hold of the beard to kiss is still customary among Arabs and Turks as a sign of friendly welcome (vid., Arvieux, <hi type="italic">Merkwürdige Nachrichten</hi>, iv. p. 182, and Harmar, <hi type="italic">Beobachtungen</hi>, ii. p. 61). The reason for this assassination was Joab’s jealousy of Amasa. Joab and Abishai then followed Sheba.
entries.6b876f77d5fb1619fa2534bbb7e7a0d77a5dcb02: <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.11">2Sa 20:11</reference> <div eID="gen4538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4539" type="x-p"/> One of Joab’s attendants remained standing by him (Amasa), no doubt at Joab’s command, and said to the people who came thither, i.e., to the men of Judah who were collected together by Amasa (vid., <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.4">2Sa 20:4</reference>), “He that favoureth Joab, and he that (is) for David, let him (go) after Joab,” i.e., follow him to battle against Sheba.
entries.7e238712ff7511fa0958b34fa1c8c6881bd310a6: <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.12-2Sam.20.13">2Sa 20:12-13</reference> <div eID="gen4539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4540" type="x-p"/> Amasa lay wallowing in blood in the midst of the road; and when the man (the attendant) saw that all the people stood still (by the corpse), he turned (pushed) Amasa from the road to the field, and threw a cloth over him, whereupon they all passed by and went after Joab.
entries.896a68cc588e8f7088209dfc5dbd4c5a20eb95dc: <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.14">2Sa 20:14</reference> <div eID="gen4540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4541" type="x-p"/> But Joab “went through all the tribes of Israel to Abela, and Beth-maacah, and all Berim.” <hi type="italic">Abela</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.20.15">2Sa 20:15</reference>), or <hi type="italic">Abel</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.20.18">2Sa 20:18</reference>), has been preserved in the large Christian village of <hi type="italic">Abil</hi>, a place with ruins, and called <hi type="italic">Abil-el-Kamh</hi> on account of its excellent wheat (<hi type="italic">Kamh</hi>), which lies to the north-west of Lake Huleh, upon a Tell on the eastern side of the river <hi type="italic">Derdâra</hi>; not in <hi type="italic">Ibl-el-Hawa</hi>, a place to the north of this, upon the ridge between <hi type="italic">Merj Ayun</hi> and <hi type="italic">Wady et Teim</hi> (vid., Ritter, <hi type="italic">Erdk</hi>. xv. pp. 240, 241; <hi type="italic">Robinson</hi>, <hi type="italic">Bibl</hi>. <hi type="italic">Researches</hi>, pp. 372-3; and v. de Velde, <hi type="italic">Mem</hi>. p. 280). <hi type="italic">Beth-maacah</hi> was quite close to Abela; so that the names of the two places are connected together in <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.15">2Sa 20:15</reference>, and afterwards, as <hi type="italic">Abel-beth-maacah</hi> (vid., 1Ki 15:20, and 2Ki 15:29), also called <hi type="italic">Abel-maim</hi> in 2Ch 16:4. <hi type="italic">Berim</hi> is the name of a district which is unknown to us; and even the early translators did not know how to render it. There is nothing, however, either in the πάντες ἐν χαῤῥί is the lxx or the <hi type="italic">omnes viri electi</hi> of the Vulgate, to warrant an alteration of the text. The latter, in fact, rests upon a mere conjecture, which is altogether unsuitable; for the subject to ויּקּהלוּ cannot be כּל־הבּרים on account of the <hi type="italic">vav consec</hi>., but must be obtained from ישׂראל בּכל־שׁבטי. The <hi type="italic">Chethib</hi> ויקלהו is evidently a slip of the pen for ויּקּהלוּ.
entries.75e745d778c73da86a0f7f8c070378ad41f4f91c: <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.15">2Sa 20:15</reference> <div eID="gen4541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4542" type="x-p"/> They besieged him (Sheba) in Abel-beth-maacah, and <hi type="italic">piled up a rampart against the city</hi>, so that <hi type="italic">it rose up by the town-moat</hi> (חל, the moat with the low wall belonging to it); and <hi type="italic">all the people with Joab destroyed to throw down the wall</hi>.
entries.3d1487b3cddd3b59b404a4bc1d79cafc97e3f77d: <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.16-2Sam.20.18">2Sa 20:16-18</reference> <div eID="gen4542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4543" type="x-p"/> Then a wise woman of the city desired to speak to Joab, and said (from the wall) to him (<reference osisRef="2Sam.20.18">2Sa 20:18</reference>), “They were formerly accustomed to say, ask Abel; and so they brought (a thing) to pass.” These words show that Abel had formerly been celebrated for the wisdom of its inhabitants.
entries.e50ceec50ffc126eaaf8a3c9e1b78ec0fe1df52a: <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.19">2Sa 20:19</reference> “I am of the peaceable, faithful in Israel: thou seekest to slay a city and mother in Israel; wherefore wilt thou destroy the inheritance of Jehovah?” The construing of אנכי with a predicate in the plural may be explained on the simple ground that the woman spoke in the name of the city as well as in its favour, and therefore had the citizens in her mind at the time, as is very evident from the figurative expression אם (mother) for mother-city or capital.<note placement="foot">The correctness of the text is not to be called in question, as Thenius and Böttcher suppose, for the simple reason that all the older translators have followed the Hebrew text, including even the lxx with their ἐγώ εἰμι εἰρηνικὰ τῶν στηριγμάτων ἐν Ἰσραήλ; whereas the words ἅ ἔθεντο οἱ πιστοὶ τοῦ Ἰσραήλ, which some of the MSS contain at the close of <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.18">2Sa 20:18</reference> after ει ̓ ἐξέλιπον, and upon which Thenius and Böttcher have founded their conjectures, are evidently a gloss or paraphrase of התמּוּ וכן, and of so little value on critical grounds, that Tischendorf did not even think the reading worth mentioning in his edition of the Septuagint.</note> <div eID="gen4543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4544" type="x-p"/> The woman gave Joab to understand, in the first place, that he ought to have asked the inhabitants of Abela whether they intended to fight for Sheba before commencing the siege and destruction of the town, according to the law laid down in Deu 20:10. with reference to the siege of foreign towns; and secondly, that he ought to have taken into consideration the peaceableness and fidelity of the citizens of Abela, and not to destroy the peace-loving citizens and members of the nation of God.
entries.8326831b7f4bb42ee702bc6aa25b049e75d9b361: <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.20">2Sa 20:20</reference> <div eID="gen4544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4545" type="x-p"/> The woman’s words made an impression upon Joab. He felt the truthfulness of her reproaches, and replied, “Far be it, far be it from me, to swallow up or destroy.” אם, as in the case of oaths: “<hi type="italic">truly not</hi>.”
entries.f07ce40086ef4657e715856d3722ece7cab7692c: <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.21">2Sa 20:21</reference> “It is not so (sc., as thou sayest), but a man of the mountains of Ephraim (which extended into the tribe of Benjamin: see at <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.1">1Sa 1:1</reference>), Sheba the son of Bichri, hath lifted up his hand against the king David. Only give him up, and I will draw away from the city.” The woman promised him this: “Behold, his head shall be thrown out to thee over the wall.”
entries.c85ff79963c40a2d01e6f85092c2611b4cbfb691: <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.22">2Sa 20:22</reference> <div eID="gen4545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4546" type="x-p"/> She then came to all the people (i.e., the citizens of the town) “<hi type="italic">with her wisdom</hi>,” i.e., with the wise counsel which she had given to Joab, and which he had accepted; whereupon the citizens cut off Sheba’s head, and threw it out to Joab. Then Joab had a trumpet blown for a retreat, and the men disbanded, whilst he himself returned to Jerusalem to the king.
entries.d2f9d6350478ca6ca75aaed7fdb6b596d7cf429c: <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.23-2Sam.20.26">2Sa 20:23-26</reference> <div eID="gen4546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4547" type="x-p"/> David’s Ministers of State. - The second section of the history of David’s reign closes, like the first (2Sa 8:16.), with a list of the leading ministers of state. The author evidently found the two lists in his sources, and included them both in his work, for the simple reason that they belonged to different periods, as the difference in the names of some of the officers clearly shows, and that they supplemented on another. The list before us belongs to a later period of David’s reign than the one in <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.16">2Sa 8:16</reference>-18. In addition to the office-bearers mentioned in 2 Samuel 8, we find here <hi type="italic">Adoram</hi> over the tribute, and <hi type="italic">Ira</hi> the Kairite a confidential counsellor (<hi type="italic">cohen</hi>: see at <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.18">2Sa 8:18</reference>), in the place of the sons of David noticed in 2Sa 8:18. The others are the same in both lists. The <hi type="italic">Chethib</hi> הכרי is to be read הכּרי (cf. 2Ki 11:4, 2Ki 11:19), from כוּר, <hi type="italic">perfodit</hi>, and is synonymous with הכּרתי (see at <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.18">2Sa 8:18</reference>). Adoram is the same person as Adoniram, who is mentioned in 1Ki 4:6 and 1Ki 5:14 as overseer over the tributary service in the time of Solomon; as we may see from the fact, that the latter is also called Adoram in 1Ki 12:18, and Hadoram in 2Ch 10:18. Hadoram is apparently only a contracted form of the name, and not merely a copyist’s mistake for Adoniram. But when we find that, according to the passage cited, the same man filled this office under three kings, we must bear in mind that he did not enter upon it till the close of David’s reign, as he is not mentioned in 2Sa 8:16., and that his name only occurs in connection with Rehoboam’s ascent of the throne; so that there is no ground for assuming that he filled the office for any length of time under that monarch. המּס does not mean <hi type="italic">vectigal</hi>, i.e., tribute or tributary service, but tributary labourers. The derivation of the word is uncertain, and has been disputed. The appointment of a special prefect over the tributary labourers can hardly have taken place before the closing years of David’s reign, when the king organized the internal administration of the kingdom more firmly than before. On the tributary labourers, see at 1Ki 5:13. Ira the Jairite is never mentioned again. There is no ground for altering <hi type="italic">Jairi</hi> (the Jairite) into <hi type="italic">Jithri</hi> (the Jithrite), as Thenius proposes, since the rendering given in the Syriac (“from Jathir”) is merely an inference from <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.38">2Sa 23:38</reference>; and the assumption upon which this conclusion is founded, viz., that <hi type="italic">Ira</hi>, the hero mentioned in <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.38">2Sa 23:38</reference>, is the same person as <hi type="italic">Ira</hi> the royal <hi type="italic">cohen</hi>, is altogether unfounded.  <chapter eID="2Sam.20"/> <div eID="gen4547" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:p>AND there happend <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">His presence was casual in it self, though certain, and ordered by God's Providence.</ns0:note> to be there a man of Belial <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">A Lawless person, one that attempted to shake off the Yoke of Civil Authority; See <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 13. 13.</ns0:note>, whose name <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> Sheba the son of Bichri, a Benjamite <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Agrieved at the Translation of the King<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom from <ns0:hi>Saul,</ns0:hi> and that Tribe, to <ns0:hi>David.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, and he blew a trumpet, and said, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Kin. 12. 16.</ns0:note> We have no part in David <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">The Tribe of <ns0:hi>Iudah</ns0:hi> have Monopolized the King to themselves, and will not allow us any share in him; let them therefore enjoy him alone, and let us seek out a new King.</ns0:note>, neither have we inheritance in the son of Jesse <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">The Tribe of <ns0:hi>Iudah</ns0:hi> have Monopolized the King to themselves, and will not allow us any share in him; let them therefore enjoy him alone, and let us seek out a new King.</ns0:note>: every man to his tents <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">An Expression of Contempt, implying their Rejection of him, that he was no more to be owned as their King, but as a private Person, as the Son of <ns0:hi>Iesse. f</ns0:hi> Let us all desist from this unthank<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful Office, of bringing the King back, and go each to our homes, that we may consider, and then meet together to chuse a New King.</ns0:note>, O Israel.</ns0:p>

                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The generality of those <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> who were pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sent.</ns0:note> went up from af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter David, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> followed Sheba the son of Bichri: but the men of Judah clave unto their king, from Jordan even to Jerusalem.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 ¶ And David came to his house at Jerusalem, and the king took the ten women <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 15. 16. and 16. 22.</ns0:note> concubines, whom he had left to keep the house, and put them in <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> a house of ward.</ns0:note> ward <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Partly, because they had not vigorously Opposed <ns0:hi>Ab<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />saloms</ns0:hi> Lustful Desire, as they should have done, even with the hazard of their Lives: and partly, lest the sight of them should renew the Memory of <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi>'s Filthiness, and of their own and <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s Reproach, which it was fit to bury in perpetual Oblivion: and partly, because it might appear Incestuous to have to do with those who had been defiled by his own Son: and partly, because as <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> would not, so it was not now convenient that any other man should have any Conjugal conversation with them.</ns0:note>, and sed them, but went not in unto them, so they were <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">

                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> in wi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dowhood of life.</ns0:note> living in widowhood.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 ¶ Then said the king to Amasa, <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> Call.</ns0:note> Assemble me the men of Judah <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">And March in the Head of them as their General, as I have promised thee; <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 19. 13.</ns0:note>, within three days <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Which he supposed <ns0:hi>Amasa</ns0:hi> having been their late General could easily do: and the business required haste.</ns0:note>, and be thou here present <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Within that time to receive Orders and Instructions from me.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 So Amasa went to assemble the <ns0:hi>men of</ns0:hi> Ju<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dah; but he tarried longer than the set time <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Either, because the people being wearied out by the late Civil War, were not forward to Engage in another: or, because the Soldiers had more Affection to <ns0:hi>Ioa<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>,</ns0:hi> than to their new General; to whose ill Conduct possibly they might impute their unsuccessfulness in the last Battel: Or, because <ns0:hi>Amasa</ns0:hi> for his own Interest might seek delays, to render himself more necessary and useful to the King, and to keep up his Honourable and Profitable Employment, which is the common Policy of such Men.</ns0:note> which he had appointed him.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 And David said to Abishai <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Not to <ns0:hi>Ioab;</ns0:hi> lest by this means he should recover his Place, and <ns0:hi>Amasa</ns0:hi> be discontented, and <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s Fidelity in making good his Promise to <ns0:hi>Amasa</ns0:hi> be questioned.</ns0:note>, Now shall She<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ba the son of Bichri do us more harm than <ns0:hi>did</ns0:hi> Absalom: take thou <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 11. 11<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                     </ns0:note> thy lords servants <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">

He speaks of him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self in the Third Person, as is very frequent. For it is not probable he would now call <ns0:hi>Ioab his lord,</ns0:hi> whom he had lately Deposed; nor <ns0:hi>Amasa,</ns0:hi> who had not yet taken actu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />al Possession of his Place, nor had the Command over the King's Guards.</ns0:note>, and pursue after him, lest he get him fenced cities, and <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> deliver himself from our eyes.</ns0:note> escape us.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 And there went out after him Joabs men <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">The remainders of <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi>'s Army who were there pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sent, with whom also <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi> might go as a Reformade, watch<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing an opportunity to do what he designed.</ns0:note>

                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:note> Cherethites, and the Pelethites <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Of whom, see on <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 8. 18.</ns0:note>, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
